notes.meaning: King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to congratulate Solomon after learning he had become king. Hiram had been a loyal friend and ally to King David for many years. David’s godly friendship had left a lasting bond of peace between the two nations.

Solomon sent a formal message to Hiram to begin plans for building the temple. He explained that his father David could not build a house for the Lord because of constant wars with surrounding enemies. David had to spend his years protecting the land until God gave him complete victory over every foe.

Solomon declared that the Lord had now given him peace and safety on every border. There were no foreign enemies attacking and no internal rebellions disturbing the nation. Solomon saw this peaceful rest as God's gift, intended to free him to do the Lord's work.

Because of this God-given peace, Solomon announced his plan to build a temple for the Lord. He was not acting out of personal ambition, but in obedience to God's promise to David that his son would build it. A house for the Lord's name meant a sacred place dedicated to God's worship and honor.

Solomon asked Hiram to order his men to cut cedar trees from the great forests of Lebanon. He offered to send his own servants to help and promised to pay whatever wages Hiram set. Solomon humbly recognized that the Phoenician foresters were far more skilled at logging and woodcraft than the people of Israel.

When Hiram received Solomon’s message, he was filled with joy and praised the Lord. He was glad that the friendship he shared with David would continue, and he praised God for giving David such a wise son. Hiram showed deep respect for the God of Israel who had blessed his neighbor so richly.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that Hiram’s praise reflects ancient royal etiquette toward an ally's deity, rather than a personal conversion to worship Israel's God alone.

notes.meaning: Hiram agreed to Solomon's request and promised to supply both cedar and cypress timber. His servants would haul the cut logs down to the Mediterranean Sea, tie them into rafts, and float them down the coast to Israel's port. In return, Hiram asked Solomon to provide food and grain supplies for the royal household of Tyre.

Hiram delivered all the cedar and cypress wood that Solomon requested for the temple. In exchange, Solomon sent a massive yearly payment of wheat and pure olive oil to feed Hiram’s court. This honest trade met the needs of both nations and showed Solomon’s fairness and wealth.

The Lord gave Solomon great wisdom in his royal leadership, just as He had promised. This wisdom led to peace between Israel and Tyre, and the two kings sealed their friendship with a formal treaty. Solomon was permitted to make this alliance because the Tyrians were not among the Canaanite nations Israel had been commanded to destroy.

Solomon called up a workforce of thirty thousand men from throughout Israel to assist in the building project. Wisely avoiding overworking them, he sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of ten thousand, allowing each man to spend two months at home for every month abroad. He placed Adoniram in charge of directing this national labor force.

Solomon also gathered seventy thousand carriers to move heavy loads and eighty thousand stonecutters to work in the mountains. A group of thirty-three hundred foremen was assigned to supervise the vast workforce and keep the work orderly. Most of these heavy laborers were foreign residents living in the land of Israel.

Solomon ordered his workers to quarry large, costly blocks of high-quality stone to lay the foundation of the temple. These stones were carefully cut and polished at the rock face so they would fit together perfectly. Even though foundation stones would remain hidden underground, Solomon spared no expense or care on what was built for God.

Solomon’s builders worked together with Hiram’s craftsmen and skilled masons from the coastal city of Gebal. They quarried the stones and shaped both the timber and rocks to make them ready for building. Commentators often see this partnership as a picture of Gentiles joining with God's people in building up His church.
